extracted.intended_audience: researchers in meta-science/scientometrics, journal editors, and practitioners studying peer review processes
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical analysis of how peer review content, reviewer/author characteristics, and manuscript revisions affect acceptance timeline and a paper's contribution potential, using open review data from PeerJ. Focuses on sentiment analysis, topic modeling of added words, and regression models to predict outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution Potential (Definition 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The contribution potential of a given paper measures how much recognition and engagement an article has currently received. We use the (1) number of citations, (2) Altmetrics and (3) number of readers as proxies for a paper’s future potential to contribute to its field. We refer to (2) and (3) collectively as a paper’s citation metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalizes 'contribution potential' as three measurable proxies (citations, Altmetrics, readers). Explicitly acknowledges these are proxies for future contribution. Use Dimensions, Altmetric API, and reader counts from reference managers to retrieve these metrics. Control for field and time when using citation counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: PeerJ reviewer evaluation aspects: Basic Reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the standard reviewer questions PeerJ asks reviewers to comment on: Basic Reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PeerJ structures reviews into fixed aspects; 'Basic Reporting' captures reporting completeness and clarity. All feedback is organized under these fixed headings, allowing scalable parsing of review content.

rubrics_metrics.name: PeerJ reviewer evaluation aspects: Experimental Design
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the standard reviewer questions PeerJ asks reviewers to comment on: Experimental Design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are asked to evaluate experimental design as an objective determination of methodological soundness rather than subjective impact. This dimension is used to assess methodological adequacy of submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PeerJ reviewer evaluation aspects: Validity of the Findings
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the standard reviewer questions PeerJ asks reviewers to comment on: Validity of the Findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dimension focuses reviewers on whether the paper's conclusions are supported by the methods and data; part of PeerJ's emphasis on scientific and methodological soundness.

rubrics_metrics.name: PeerJ reviewer evaluation aspects: Comments for the Author
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the standard reviewer questions PeerJ asks reviewers to comment on: Comments for the Author (contains miscellaneous and specific comments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Comments for the Author' captures free-text, miscellaneous, and specific suggestions; many detailed reviewer remarks are located here and are the primary source for text-sentiment and revision-guidance analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review content (dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review content — the textual content of peer reviewers' feedback; the study focuses on the sentiment of review content and whether reviewers sign their reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure polarity and subjectivity of reviewer comments (TextBlob polarity in (−1,1); subjectivity in (0,1)). Compare sentiment for reviewers who 'sign' reviews versus those who remain anonymous. Use sentiment as a predictor/control in models of acceptance and contribution potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of review iterations (dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of rounds of revision that the article underwent (each submission version increments by 0.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count rounds of revision as a variable (number_of_revisions) to test whether more revisions are associated with acceptance speed or future citation impact. Use mixed-effects models to control for research-area heterogeneity when relating number of revisions to citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review editor decision (dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor's final decision after peer reviewers' feedback: reject, request minor or major revision, or accept the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model editor decisions using conditional mixed logit models, controlling for research area fixed effects and covariates such as author gender, h-index, review sentiment, and citation metrics. Note dataset includes only papers eventually accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript modifications (dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific changes authors make to manuscripts between revisions (words added or removed; this study focuses on words added in the first revision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extract textual differences between contiguous submission versions by word counts to identify 'added' and 'removed' words. Represent added-words as documents for LDA topic modeling (bag-of-words), remove rare words appearing in fewer than ~50 documents, and interpret topics using coherence and perplexity to choose topic counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polarity of reviewers’ comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Polarity score of reviewers' comments (TextBlob polarity in (−1,1) where negative values mean negative sentiment and positive values correspond to positive sentiment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use polarity as an independent or control variable in regression models predicting acceptance and sentiment effects. Robustness checks: replicate using alternate sentiment tools (e.g., Vader, NLTK). Also consider variance of polarity across reviewers for a paper as a proxy for controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjectivity of reviewers’ comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjectivity score returned by TextBlob (range 0–1, higher values indicate higher subjectivity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subjectivity to study differences between signed and anonymous reviews (signed reviews found to be more subjective). Note: some sentiment tools (e.g., NLTK Vader) may not produce subjectivity scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variance of reviewers’ polarity (controversy proxy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Variance of polarity of the individual reviewer comments for a paper, used as a proxy measurement for the degree of controversy of the review for that paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include variance of polarity in models to capture disagreement among reviewers. Used in some models to test whether higher controversy affects editor decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polarity of authors’ rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: Polarity score of the authors’ rebuttal/response letters (TextBlob polarity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include as a control variable in models predicting editor decisions and subsequent outcomes, under the hypothesis that authors' tone or sentiment in rebuttals may influence reviewer/editor perceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors' h-index as prestige metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Use authors' h-index (maximum h-index among authors; average h-index of authors) as a proxy for prestige or reputation in academia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include maximum and average h-index as predictors of acceptance speed and as controls for citation outcomes. Note limitation: h-index values used are current at data retrieval, not necessarily at time of submission; authors acknowledge temporal mismatch and test robustness on restricted subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author gender variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Author gender indicators: Female last author (dummy), Female 1st author (dummy), Female author ratio (proportion of female authors). Gender inferred via Genderize.io.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include gender variables to test for gender effects on editor decisions and reviewer sentiment. Acknowledge gender is not binary and inference has limitations. Use cross-terms (e.g., female author ratio × reviewer anonymity) to examine interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name revealed reviewer (signed review) indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Dummy variable that is 1 if the reviewer reveals his or her name (signs the review) after publication, otherwise 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to compare sentiment and subjectivity between signed and anonymous reviews; signed reviewers in this dataset wrote more positive and subjective reviews, implying social pressure effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control variables for modeling citation outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Include number of authors, research area (as random intercepts or dummies), year-month trend (months since publication), and article dummy variables as controls when modeling citation counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control for field heterogeneity (random intercepts by research area), time since publication (linear trend) and author visibility (h-index) to isolate effects of review-process variables on citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting added/removed words as a method for revision analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Find differences between contiguous submission versions by counting occurrences of words to identify words 'added' (present in current revision but not previous) and 'removed' (vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method loses word ordering but is compatible with bag-of-words topic modeling (LDA). Focus analysis on words added during first revision; interpret added words categories (e.g., hedging words like 'however', 'may') as indicative of changes in implication or bounds on claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: LDA topic modeling of added-words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) on the documents composed of words added in a revision to discover categories of manuscript modifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select number of topics based on perplexity and coherence (seek low perplexity and high coherence). Remove rare words (appear in < ~1% of documents) to mitigate topic contamination by specific technical terms. Interpret topics qualitatively to understand kinds of changes (e.g., analysis, hedging).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mixed-effects regression to account for heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use mixed linear regression models and conditional mixed logit models to account for heterogeneity across research areas and to estimate fixed effects across reviews or articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In modeling acceptance decisions and citation counts, incorporate random effects (e.g., research-area intercepts) to control for differing baseline behaviors across fields and use fixed effects for covariates of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization of 'review robustness' (cited standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review robustness operationalized in prior work as the lack of influence of extrinsic variables (e.g., area of research, type of peer review, reviewer gender) on linguistic characteristics of peer reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider 'review robustness' as a quality dimension: fewer associations between extrinsic variables and review language implies more robust review outcomes. The paper cites Buljan et al. (2020) as an example of this operationalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency as proxy for peer-review quality (cited standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use transparency of the peer review process as a proxy for review quality (Wicherts 2016 developed a 14-item scale measuring transparency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize existing tools that measure transparency as a component of review quality. The paper notes heterogeneity in existing quality-assessment tools and the limitations of self-report measures.
